speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To this end, we have built up a suite of well-regarded international dispute resolution services – the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC), the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC) as well as the Singapore International Mediation Centre (SIMC).

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have also bolstered our infrastructure significantly to support the growing demand for these services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Most recently, the opening of the Maxwell Chambers Suites has tripled Maxwell Chambers' size in terms of offerings for venues for dispute resolution, meeting places and also working spaces.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Integral to effective international dispute resolution is the ability to enforce judgments, awards and settlements not just in the countries where they were obtained but also in the countries where the parties' assets are located.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For businesses and investors, enhanced frameworks for cross-border recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments, awards and settlements would increase legal certainty and reduce the costs and uncertainties associated with cross-border dealings and disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singapore actively participates in and supports the development of appropriate multilateral frameworks for the enforcement of judgments, awards and settlements resulting from international dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are parties to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements and the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of foreign court judgments in civil proceedings which fall outside of the Hague Convention framework, Singapore's existing legislative framework consists of two Acts – the Reciprocal Enforcement of Commonwealth Judgments Act or RECJA, and the Reciprocal Enforcement of Foreign Judgments Act or REFJA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These Acts have not been updated since their enactment under the British colonial administration, and the number of jurisdictions under Singapore's reciprocal enforcement of judgments regime is very low.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Further, only money judgments from superior courts of recognised jurisdictions may be enforced by registration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Money judgments from other foreign jurisdictions may still be enforced by common law, but this would entail commencing a fresh action in Singapore to enforce a debt, which may then be costlier and also more time-consuming.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This route would obviously not be desirable for foreign litigants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singapore has a vision to be the premier dispute resolution hub in Asia, if not the world.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As mentioned earlier, we have developed a comprehensive range of institutions and infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of our legal regime, we have entered into a network of international agreements so as to enhance the recognition and enforcement of judgments, awards and settlement agreements from Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is therefore timely that we supplement the existing regime to further strengthen Singapore's value proposition for litigants considering where to resolve their disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Comparable Commonwealth jurisdictions, such as the United Kingdom (UK), Australia and New Zealand, have already expanded their regimes to cover more types of civil judgments, or civil judgments from more tiers of courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill seeks to bring our legislation in line with international developments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First, the new framework expands the scope of reciprocal arrangements that Singapore can enter into with foreign countries, by allowing more types of judgments to be covered by these arrangements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As mentioned earlier, currently, the scope of judgments that such arrangements can cover is limited.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Only two main types of judgments are covered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think the legal practitioners in this House will know that the Act covers final money judgments given by foreign superior courts in civil proceedings, which would, in this case, include foreign judgments that might be based on a right of action conferred by a regulatory statute but otherwise provides for compensation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is the compensatory aspect that would also be caught in the current regime.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Penal orders, punitive fines and confiscation or forfeiture orders made in criminal proceedings do not fall within the present or the proposed – if this Bill is passed – scope of REFJA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we will bring in four more types of judgments in civil proceedings into the fold recognised by REFJA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will enable litigants to realise a fuller range of remedies granted by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Non-money judgments include: (a) freezing orders, injunctions which prevent a party from dealing with assets, to ensure that assets remain available to satisfy an eventual money judgment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if a party has assets in Singapore and there is a freezing injunction that is ordered in the foreign country, if it is under REFJA, this will then be brought into the fold as well; (b) injunctions which require a party to do or to refrain from doing an act; and finally (c) orders for specific performance which require a party to perform the obligations under a contract, usually to complete a sale and purchase or some other matter where the proceeds or the item that is sought is of intrinsic value.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ordinarily, the judgment creditor of a foreign non-money judgment seeking recognition and enforcement of this judgment requires the Singapore Courts' assistance so that the orders in the foreign judgment may be effected in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There may, however, be practical difficulties, or issues of policy and convenience in recognising and enforcing foreign non-money judgments, especially if given by a court from a different legal system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If the Court is of the opinion that such enforcement would not be just and convenient, then the Court may order the registration of such amount as it considers to be the money equivalent of the relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If a Court considers that the recognition of an order which requires the doing of an Act or the refraining from doing of an Act is not just and convenient, then the Court would consider what is an equivalent monetary value and order that in its place.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For instance, where the Court finds that it would not be just and convenient to grant specific performance or an injunction, it may then grant damages in lieu of the relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Damages may be assessed on a compensatory or restitutionary basis, in accordance with established principles on assessment of damages, so as to arrive at a fair equivalent of what is lost by the refusal of the non-money relief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In doing so, the Court would consider the value of the foreign non-money relief being effected in Singapore, given that what the judgment creditor seeks is for the non-money relief to be effected in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will also open the doors for judgments from our State Courts to be enforced overseas, the Bill being reciprocal in nature.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This will strengthen the enforceability of judgments, including by ensuring that assets are not dissipated before a final judgment is obtained so that the successful claimants are not left with only a "paper" judgment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This ties in with my earlier point, where injunctions sometimes, instead of being final in nature, are also interim or interlocutory in nature.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This Bill also contemplates the recognition of this type of judgments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The ability to enforce Singapore interlocutory judgments in foreign jurisdictions, in other words, the converse, will enhance the attractiveness of Singapore Courts to litigants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Fourth, judicial settlements, consent judgments and consent orders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Arrangements between parties concluded before a Court to end the Court proceedings should equally be recognised and enforced like a judgment so as to afford parties certainty of finality in their disputes and to respect the parties' binding commitment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This amendment will also bring the regime under the REFJA in line with that under the Choice of Court Agreements Act, which recognises and enforces judicial settlements, consent judgments and consent orders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These reforms provide the broad statutory framework for Singapore to negotiate reciprocal enforcement agreements or arrangements with foreign countries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, the precise scope of enforceable judgments will be decided and negotiated with each foreign country individually.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the fact that we have the Bill being passed into the Act, does not automatically mean that there will be a whole series of countries that will come on board.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What will happen thereafter is, armed with these amendments, we will then proceed to negotiate with foreign countries, and decide in the case of each country, what is suitable, what is appropriate and, obviously, on a reciprocal basis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The factors that will be taken into account will include factors, such as the compatibility of our respective court systems – Singapore's and the foreign courts' – the needs of users of our Court systems and, of course, our countries' respective interests.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This means that while the reformed REFJA will provide a broad menu of options available for negotiation, Singapore might enter into an agreement or arrangement with Country A for the reciprocal enforcement of only a limited category of judgments, whereas with Country B, there could be reciprocal enforcement of the full range of judgments under REFJA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It really depends on what is also being negotiated and what is also being offered by the reciprocal country.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, to ensure that the requirement for reciprocity is not circumvented or bypassed, the Bill provides that some types of foreign judgments will not be recognised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, if a judgment is given by a recognised court, on appeal from a court that is not a recognised court, in other words, it is an appeal, but it originates from a court that is not a recognised Court, then this will not be recognised under the framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Or, conversely, where a judgment registered or enforced in a recognised court but which originated from a court that Singapore has no reciprocal enforcement arrangements with, will also fall outside the scope of the framework.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Reciprocating countries currently recognised by RECJA are expected to be transferred over to the REFJA regime before the RECJA Repeal Bill comes into force, so it will be consolidated into one common Reciprocal Enforcement Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By facilitating the realisation of judgments into real, tangible benefits even if these need to be realised overseas.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially important in a world where cross-border business transactions frequently occur and where assets and goods may be dispersed around the globe.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Enforcement via a registration of judgment is a regime that allows for cost-savings and greater certainty when an overseas judgment is being enforced.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is based on reciprocity, that is, that Singapore's judgments will be recognised and enforced in their jurisdiction and that that jurisdiction's judgment will be recognised and enforced in Singapore except for a few exceptions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This reciprocity is based on executive action, namely, through the Minister making an order under section 3 of the Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At this stage, Sir, allow me to declare that I am a practising lawyer at the Singapore Bar.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill streamlines and broadens the regime, furthering Singapore's position as a dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because our judgments will be more easily enforced overseas, parties will have greater reason to choose Singapore to resolve the dispute.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As more cases in Singapore are heard, Singapore's jurisprudence will develop.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With more established jurisprudence and greater familiarity with Singapore law, more contracting parties will choose Singapore law as the choice of law and Singapore as the place with exclusive jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill streamlines the regime by removing the distinction between Commonwealth and non-Commonwealth countries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although they operated in generally the same way, there were a few minor differences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the tests for setting aside registration of a judgment on grounds of public policy are slightly different in section 5(a)(v) of the Reciprocal Enforcement of Foreign Judgment Act and section 2(f) of the Reciprocal Enforcement of Commonwealth Judgment Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This streamlined statutory regime supplements other processes by which foreign judgments are enforced in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, it does not include recognition and enforcement of interim measures.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The statutory regime, as amended by this Bill, will allow such reciprocal recognition if and when such bilateral agreements are entered into.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides formalised statutory procedures, there are also non-binding memoranda between countries that help facilitate this process of recognition and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One such example is the Memorandum of Guidance Between The Supreme People's Court of The People's Republic of China and The Supreme Court of Singapore on Recognition and Enforcement of Money Judgments In Commercial Cases signed on 31 August 2018.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Relevant to how the Reciprocal Enforcement of Foreign Judgment Act supplements and does not affect other existing regimes, would the Minister explain the rationale behind the retention of section 7(1) of the Reciprocal Enforcement of Foreign Judgment Act which says that "no proceedings for the recovery of a sum payable under a foreign judgment, being a judgment to which this Part applies, other than proceedings by way of registration of the judgment, shall be entertained by any Court in Singapore"?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Does this mean that if a judgment could be enforced via the Choice of Court Act instead of the REFJA, that the REFJA must be resorted to and not the Choice of Court Act?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As this streamlined statutory regime supplements existing regimes, this Bill also broadens the scope of the Act, making it more useful.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although retaining the limitations of certain kinds of judgments in section 2(2), clause 2 includes non-money judgement as a type of judgment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is very helpful even for commercial matters.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, in cases involving intellectual property rights, the remedy may be to transfer property or to destroy infringing material.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Coupled with the inclusion of interlocutory judgments as a type of judgment recognised by the Act in clause 2, global mareva injunctions can be registered and enforced without commencing a separate action.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because there may be differences in legal remedies available or some other reasons where it may be just and convenient not to strictly enforce a non-money judgment, the new section 4(3A)(b) gives the Court discretion on how to enforce non-money judgments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The previous blanket ban against recognition of Subordinate Courts prevented Singapore's State Court judgments from being registered overseas due to the need for reciprocity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because of the increase in jurisdictional limit of the State Courts, cases that have to be enforced overseas have to be transferred to the High Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The party who needs overseas enforcement may not get High Court costs from the other party, incurring greater unrecoverable costs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, this change to make it possible for Singapore to enter into bilateral agreements that recognise judgments from our State Courts directly is ideal.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even while this Bill expands the possibilities for enforcing judgments and interim measures from other jurisdictions, this Bill also puts in safeguards to prevent abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: According to the Explanatory Statement, an example of this is in the event of a bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This prevents the bankruptcy regime from being circumvented.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With more possibilities albeit with in-built safeguards, there will be greater flexibility to negotiate bilateral agreements on the recognition and enforcement of Court judgments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: No changes seem to have been made to the list of countries under the REFJA and RECJA at least since 1999.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hopefully, more bilateral agreements to this effect would be entered into following this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would boost dispute resolution in Singapore as the ability to enforce a judgment in multiple countries can be valuable for certain commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Though I cannot help but notice the slight tinge of irony that the well-used REFJA is being repealed in our Bicentennial Year, nevertheless, for a good reason, I guess.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How does it intend to proactively reach out to other countries to obtain agreement on reciprocal recognition and enforcement of each other's civil judgments for the purposes of the consolidated REFJA?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, may I also ask the Senior Minister of State, based on past experiences, what are the common factors preventing Singapore from reaching agreement with other jurisdictions on reciprocal recognition and enforcement of civil judgments?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, if so, how does the Senior Minister of State expect that the Government will work towards overcoming these difficulties?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, does the Senior Minister of State think that this is something that is workable at some point?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And what will be some of the challenges anticipated?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These two Bills are presented after public consultation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The move on the part of the Ministry of Law to consult before introducing these two Bills is to be commended.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The stated aims of these Bills are to streamline the statutory regimes for the recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments into one under REFJA and to take the necessary steps to ensure the recognition of Singapore's civil judgments overseas on the basis of the reciprocity principle between countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As mentioned by the hon Senior Minister of State, Singapore is already a well-recognised dispute resolution hub, with the SIAC, SICC and SIMC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the context of the litigation in Courts, the setting up of SICC was a game changer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: SICC, a division of the High Court, consists of top international jurists, in addition to the Singapore Supreme Court judges, who all have deep expertise, skill and experience to try complex international commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore's ratification of the Convention on Choice of Court Agreements, a point that the hon Member, Mr Christopher de Souza mentioned, allows judgments issued by the Singapore Court pursuant to exclusive choice of Court agreements to be recognised by signatory countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The effect of this is to allow a Singapore judgment to be similarly recognised by competent authorities in foreign jurisdictions through the reciprocity principle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Subject to the comments that I will shortly make, I support the enlargement of the statutory base.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before I deal with my comments on the Bills, I would like to make some suggestions on steps that can be considered to increase the attraction of Singapore's Courts judgments and Singapore as a dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had previously suggested in this House that Singapore consider the viability of entering into the Apostille Convention which deals with certification of a document's validity for legal purposes in signatory states.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are currently 117 countries which are parties to this Convention.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would significantly cut down the costs and labour involved in legalisation of documents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that the Ministry of Law is looking into this matter and would appreciate an update.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the same vein, I would suggest that the Government consider the viability of Singapore signing the Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil and Commercial Matters, in other words, the Hague Service Convention, which currently has 75 countries as contracting parties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will enable easier service of process commencing legal action on parties situated in Convention countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, it may take an inordinate amount of time through the usual consular routes to serve process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this may take between three to five years, depending on the countries involved.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Returning to the Bills, I would like to ask about the scope of recognition and enforcement of an interim and non-money judgment under the proposed amendments to REFJA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note from the hon Senior Minister of State's speech that injunctions are considered; also, orders for specific performance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is to be welcomed because previously, in my view, there was a "black hole" which a defendant can exploit because the individual may be situated in one country and have assets in another country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The current legal position in Singapore is that the local Courts may not necessarily grant an injunctive relief purely in aid of foreign proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In an interconnected world, this makes less sense and, certainly, it is not the case in respect of arbitration proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the International Arbitration Act, the Singapore Court may issue interim relief in respect of arbitration proceedings overseas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, with this amendment, we can potentially resolve this anomaly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And through the principle of reciprocity, I hope that the Singapore interim judgments will similarly be recognised overseas so as not to render a subsequent final judgment of the Singapore Courts nugatory.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to civil forfeiture action taken by sovereign governments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are certain jurisdictions which assert wide jurisdiction over assets wherever it may be situated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this may also be seen as a sidestep from what would otherwise be the subject matter of a mutual legal assistance treaty (MLAT) request between countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There could also be issues vis-a-vis bona fide third parties who may have to deal with assets that are ordered to be forfeited by a foreign court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, it may be useful to consider how other jurisdictions deal with such orders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, in New Jersey, there is a separate piece of legislation dealing with civil asset recovery orders made by foreign courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about section 7(1) of REFJA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The rationale for having and retaining this provision is to preclude judgment creditors from seeking to enforce such foreign judgments, which are contemplated and covered by REFJA, under the common law route.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if you have a judgment that fits within REFJA's framework, then do it by way of registration and not take up Court time and seek to deploy the common law recognition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As for foreign judgments that may be recognised and enforced under the Choice of Court Agreement, these will continue to be excluded from the reformed REFJA under section 2A of REFJA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if the parties have chosen by agreement a Court, the convention applies, and you use the Choice of Court Agreements Act to recognise those judgments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza also asked about plans to negotiate new reciprocal arrangements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Dennis Tan also asked several questions in this regard.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The purpose behind the amendments is to first level up in terms of the options that we have, the availability of non-money judgments, for example, to be recognised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Based on this, what will happen is that we have to look at the regimes in other countries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Having regard to what Singapore's business interest would be, what serves Singapore lawyers, the Singapore business community and our interest as a whole best is in looking out for the countries that we might want to have an arrangement with, that will be the driving consideration when we look at how we negotiate and with whom we negotiate these reciprocal arrangements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will study their systems and we will look at them in the context of whether their system is also something that fits with what we regard as a proper legal system and also look at the nature and type of remedies and, therefore, judgments that they have, and the grounds and principles on which they arrive at those judgments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ultimately, we have to remember that we have to serve the public interest in Singapore, what I mentioned earlier, and those will be the principal considerations as we do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, whether as Mr Dennis Tan says it is with ASEAN or with any other country in the world on this, those will be the considerations that we will have.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of Mr Murali Pillai's questions on the scope of recognition and the enforcement, I think there were two questions on this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The first is what kinds of interim and non-money judgments are contemplated to be recognised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I outlined earlier the types that are considered, so freezing orders, Mareva injunctions and so on, to preserve, on the interim basis, sometimes it is also a final injunction – the parties' assets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Injunctions requiring a party to do something, which is a mandatory injunction, or to refrain from doing something else.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Orders for specific performance could also be considered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai raised this point about declaratory judgments, those can also be recognised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We also contemplate that orders for delivery up or the recovery of property can be recognised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But one has to also be clear that this only applies to civil judgments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if one is looking at delivery up or enforcement on the property, in the context of a regulatory, penal regime or in a criminal matter, then those will not be covered by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In that context, Mr Murali Pillai also asked about civil forfeiture actions taken by sovereign governments.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The present framework, which is pre-amendment, does not cover confiscation or forfeiture orders by which assets are seized by a foreign government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reforms that we propose in this Bill do not change that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Even if some of these foreign proceedings may be classified, as a matter of labelling, as "civil", they are effectively in substance the enforcement of the foreign country's penal, revenue or public criminal laws.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those would not be caught under this Act and would not be enforced in this way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Mr Murali Pillai also pointed out, in Singapore, the enforcement of foreign confiscation orders is dealt with under the Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act (MACMA), which has the necessary safeguards in place for such requests.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under MACMA, requests for enforcement of foreign confiscation orders have to be made through the appropriate foreign authorities to the Attorney-General and dealt with in accordance with the Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked what is a "just and convenient" test in the context of the Bill, and also for an elaboration on the factors that a Court might consider before deciding that it is just and convenient to recognise a foreign money judgment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned earlier, we frame the way in which this would work without prescribing the factors to the Court, to leave some room for discretion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The “just and convenient” test has itself been developed judicially in the context of enforcement under the RECJA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Courts, in that context, have looked at factors, such as whether there was a delay and whether the delay had caused any prejudice to the judgment debtor, for instance; whether the judgment creditor could give a reasonable explanation for the delay in applying to register the judgment; whether the judgment creditor had been reasonably diligent in seeking to enforce it; and what is the conduct of the judgment debtor as well, has he been obstructive, and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are factors that are taken into account but those would not be the only factors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The overarching question and consideration for the Court to determine was, where did the interests of justice lie, having regard to the factual matrix of the case?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Member will be familiar with judicial authorities that espouse those principles and elaborate on them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If a judgment practically only applies to that country, then it would not be just and convenient to also enforce it in the context of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Another scenario would be the enforcement of the non-money judgment where that scenario could expose a person to the risk of committing an illegality or to an action for breach of a rule of privilege, for example.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, there is an unintended but consequential impact in terms of the enforcement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those might also be circumstances where it is not just and convenient.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There could also be potentially situations where the non-money judgment has got no equivalent in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will then, of course, not be just and convenient for the local Court to enforce it, given that such remedy either does not exist or is not recognised in this form from the foreign courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I hasten to add that the categories are not closed, and we leave the Court some room to decide whether in the context of the appropriate case and the parties, and the background circumstances of the case, whether it is just and convenient to recognise the foreign court's judgment and enforce it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It focuses it into one recognised format, rather than have to deal with two different statutes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On Mr Dennis Tan's point, yes, it is the Bicentennial Year, but we have never let history get in the way of good efficient governance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, Mr Murali Pillai raised two other points which he has raised in the past, the Apostille Convention and also the Hague Service Convention, those are valid points.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What I can say is that we are not averse to it, we continue to study them closely, and there are several factors which go behind the consideration of those conventions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have been busy with some other convention, but when there is an appropriate update on this, we will let the Member know.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, on that, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I beg to move.      .
